explain.say: Your teacher says, Get your book, open to page ten, and draw a tree. Three things! Words can float away fast. Look at the board. Here are five tricks to catch them.

explain.say: See the speech bubble? Say it back. Whisper the steps to yourself, Book, page ten, tree. Your own voice helps the words stick. Can you whisper them now?

explain.say: Now the hand lights up. Count on your fingers. One finger for book, two for page ten, three for tree. Your fingers hold the steps for you. How many fingers do you need?

explain.say: See the eye? Picture it. Make a little film in your head. You open your book, find page ten, and draw a tree. Pictures are easy for brains to keep. Can you see your tree?

explain.say: Last trick, do it, and ask if you forget. You can say, Can you say it again, please? That is clever, not silly. Well done! Here is a challenge. Ask someone to give you three steps, and try all the tricks.

faq.a: Your brain holds spoken words for only a short time. Lots of brains drop them quickly. Tricks like saying them back help them stay.
asks: Tell me about Look and listen

faq.q: How do I say it back?
faq.a: Quietly repeat the steps in your own words, like book, page ten, tree. You can whisper or say it in your head.
asks: Tell me about Say it back

faq.a: Ask. You can say, Can you say it again, please? or Can you write it down for me? Asking is a smart thing to do.
asks: Tell me about Do it, then ask

faq.q: Can my teacher write the steps down?
faq.a: Yes, many teachers will. You can say, Can I have the steps on paper, please? A grown-up you trust can help you ask.

faq.q: What if there are too many steps?
faq.a: Do the first one or two, then ask for the rest. You can also look at what a friend is doing for a clue.

facts: Working memory is the part of thinking that holds information for a short time.
Saying words out loud and making pictures in your head are both well-known memory helpers.

quiz.say: Your teacher gives three steps. Which trick helps?
quiz.show: Which trick helps with three steps?
quiz.why: One finger for each step helps you hold all three.

wrong.1: Covering your ears means you cannot hear the steps.
wrong.2: Looking away makes the words float off.

quiz.say: You forgot step two. What can you say?
quiz.show: You forgot step two. What can you say?

options.show: Can you say it again, please?
options.say: Can you say it again, please?

quiz.why: Asking again is smart. It gets you the step you need.

wrong.1: Guessing can lead to the wrong job. Asking is better.
wrong.2: No need to give up. One question fixes it.
